title: Reflexive pronouns and verbs
goal: Choose matching reflexive pronouns and use common reflexive verbs when the object is the subject or the verb requires reflexive use.

objectives.statement: Choose matching reflexive pronouns and use common reflexive verbs when the object is the subject or the verb requires reflexive use.

spans.value: Maja, Jonas, and Nora are leaving for a birthday party. Their bus departs soon, but not everyone is ready.
Klokka er halv seks! Vi må skynde oss.

blocks.translation: It’s half past five! We have to hurry.

spans.value: Jeg er nesten klar. Jeg vasker meg bare.

blocks.translation: I’m almost ready. I’m just washing.

spans.value: Etterpå må du kle på deg. Bussen går om tjue minutter.

blocks.translation: After that, you have to get dressed. The bus leaves in twenty minutes.

spans.value: Jeg vet det. Har Nora gjort seg klar?

blocks.translation: I know. Has Nora got ready?

spans.value: Hun kler på seg nå. Hun gleder seg til festen.

blocks.translation: She’s getting dressed now. She’s looking forward to the party.

spans.value: Nå er jeg klar! Skal dere sette dere nå?

blocks.translation: Now I’m ready! Are you going to sit down now?

spans.value: Ja, vi setter oss bare et øyeblikk.

blocks.translation: Yes, we’re just sitting down for a moment.

spans.value: Et øyeblikk? Hvis vi ikke skynder oss, mister vi bussen.

blocks.translation: A moment? If we don’t hurry, we’ll miss the bus.

spans.value: Everyone in this scene is using one of the reflexive constructions taught here: Jonas washes himself, Nora dresses herself, and Jonas and Maja sit themselves down. These constructions express the relationship with reflexive pronouns. Some common verbs also require a reflexive pronoun for their intended meaning, as in å glede seg til noe — to look forward to something.
The practical goal is to choose a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject and to use it with common reflexive verbs.

sections.title: When the subject and object refer to the same person

spans.value: In the washing, dressing, and sitting constructions taught here, a reflexive pronoun (refleksivt pronomen) is used when the object refers back to the subject.
The subject jeg and the object meg refer to the same person.
Compare this with an ordinary object:
Here, jeg and bilen do not refer to the same thing, so no reflexive pronoun is needed.
The same contrast appears with other subjects:
English often leaves out myself, yourself, or themselves when the meaning is obvious. Norwegian commonly keeps the reflexive pronoun.
A more literal translation would be I dress myself, but get dressed is more natural English.
The reflexive pronoun must match the subject:
Notice that only third-person subjects use seg.
A compact rule is:
Choose the reflexive pronoun from the subject: jeg–meg, du–deg, han/hun–seg, vi–oss, dere–dere, de–seg.
Do not choose the pronoun according to the nearest noun or according to gender. It always points back to the subject.
Nora is feminine, but the reflexive form is still seg. Norwegian does not have separate reflexive forms corresponding to English himself and herself.

sections.title: Choosing the pronoun from the subject

spans.value: Return to the party scene:
Each reflexive pronoun follows the subject. If the subject changes, the pronoun changes too.
Singular situation.
Plural situation.
Singular situation.
Plural situation.
Singular situation.
Plural situation.
The form seg can refer to one third-person subject or several:

en.value: Erik sits down by the window.

no.value: Erik og Nora setter seg ved vinduet.

en.value: Erik and Nora sit down by the window.

spans.value: The subject tells you whether seg means himself, herself, itself, or themselves.

sections.title: A common mistake: using seg with every subject

spans.value: Because seg is common, learners sometimes use it after jeg, du, vi, or dere. That is incorrect.
Incorrect:
Correct:
Incorrect:
Correct:
Seg belongs with third-person subjects such as han, hun, Nora, barna, or de. It does not function as one universal word for self.

sections.title: Common reflexive verbs in everyday routines

spans.value: Some verbs are especially common with reflexive pronouns. Learn the infinitive with seg, but change the pronoun when the subject changes.

sections.title: å vaske seg — to wash oneself, to wash

en.value: The children wash after football practice.

spans.value: The verb can also take an ordinary object:
Use the reflexive form when the object is the same person as the subject.

sections.title: å kle på seg — to get dressed

no.value: Jonas kler på seg på badet.

en.value: Jonas gets dressed in the bathroom.

no.value: Vi kler på oss før vi går ut.

en.value: We get dressed before we go out.

spans.value: Compare:
In the first sentence, Nora dresses herself. In the second, she dresses someone else.

sections.title: å gjøre seg klar — to get ready

no.value: Jeg gjør meg klar til jobb.
De gjør seg klare til festen.

en.value: They get ready for the party.

spans.value: The pronoun still follows the subject:

sections.title: å sette seg — to sit down

en.value: She sits down at the table.

no.value: Vi setter oss på setene våre på bussen.

en.value: We sit down in our seats on the bus.

spans.value: Å sette seg describes moving into a seated position. The reflexive pronoun is part of this common expression.
Compare:

en.value: Jonas sits down on the chair.
Jonas puts the cup on the table.

spans.value: The second sentence has an ordinary object, koppen. Jonas is not putting himself on the table.

sections.title: Verbs that require reflexive use for a particular meaning

spans.value: With some verbs, the reflexive form gives a familiar meaning that should be learned as a whole expression.
In the dialogue, Maja says:
Do not treat seg as a fixed part that remains unchanged. The dictionary form is å skynde seg, but an actual sentence must match the pronoun to the subject.

sections.title: å glede seg til — to look forward to

en.value: Nora is looking forward to the party.
I’m looking forward to the weekend.
We’re looking forward to the holiday.
Are you looking forward to the concert?

spans.value: The reflexive pronoun comes before til:

en.value: She is looking forward to the visit.

spans.value: The complete useful pattern is:
subject + gleder + matching reflexive pronoun + til + event or thing
Do not omit the reflexive pronoun in this meaning.
Incorrect:

en.value: ✗ I’m looking forward to the holiday.

spans.value: Correct:

en.value: I’m looking forward to the holiday.

spans.value: Changing or removing the reflexive pronoun can change the meaning of a verb, not merely its grammar.

en.value: The children are looking forward to the film.

spans.value: The lesson’s practical point is not to analyze every possible meaning of glede. It is to recognize and use å glede seg til as a complete everyday expression.
A useful question for the washing, dressing, and sitting contrasts taught here is:
Does the object refer to the same person or people as the subject?
If yes, use the matching reflexive pronoun in these taught constructions.
If no, use an ordinary object.
Compare these pairs carefully:

en.value: They sit down on the sofa.
They put the food on the table.

spans.value: The verb alone does not always decide between the taught reflexive and ordinary-object contrasts. In these contrasts, meaning decides: ask who receives the action.
When a name is the subject
A person’s name works like han or hun, so use seg.
Two or more named people also take seg because they correspond to de.

no.value: Maja og Jonas gjør seg klare.
Nora og Maja gleder seg til festen.

en.value: Nora and Maja are looking forward to the party.

spans.value: Do not replace seg with oss merely because the sentence describes several people. Use oss when the subject includes the speaker, as in vi or a coordinated subject such as Maja og jeg. Third-person subjects such as Nora og Maja use seg.

en.value: We are looking forward to the party.
They are looking forward to the party.

sections.title: Back to Maja, Jonas, and Nora

spans.value: The group finally reaches the bus stop.
Jeg gleder meg til å se alle på festen.

blocks.translation: I’m looking forward to seeing everyone at the party.

spans.value: Jeg også. Men nå må jeg sette meg litt.

blocks.translation: Me too. But now I need to sit down for a moment.

spans.value: Du kan sette deg på et sete når vi er på bussen. Nå må vi skynde oss!

blocks.translation: You can sit down in a seat when we’re on the bus. Now we have to hurry!

spans.value: Se, bussen kommer. Vi gjorde oss klare akkurat i tide.

blocks.translation: Look, the bus is coming. We got ready just in time.

spans.value: The same forms now serve different purposes within one situation:

items.value: Nora uses meg because the subject is jeg.
Jonas also uses meg after jeg.
Maja uses deg because she speaks to du.
The group uses oss because the subject is vi.

spans.value: The ending would not work naturally if every speaker used seg. Each reflexive pronoun must follow its own subject.

prompt.value: Write the matching reflexive pronoun after each subject: jeg, du, hun, vi, dere, and de. Then write one short Norwegian sentence about getting ready with «gjøre seg klar» or «kle på seg», and one short Norwegian sentence about looking forward to an everyday event with «glede seg til». Inflect each reflexive pronoun to match its subject.

payload.judge_prompt: Check the response against the task and report evidence for each criterion. Accept natural Bokmål variants with correct subject–pronoun agreement. For the two sentences, accept natural wording that uses the required complete reflexive expressions.

criteria.instruction: Gives the correct reflexive pronouns for all six subjects: jeg–meg, du–deg, hun–seg, vi–oss, dere–dere, and de–seg.
Writes one short Norwegian sentence about getting ready using a complete taught reflexive expression, such as gjøre seg klar or kle på seg.
Writes one short Norwegian sentence about looking forward to an everyday event using the complete expression glede seg til.
